articles.label: Analysis
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Stormwater Problem Has No Fix in Sight
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a dedicated fee, the county has spent more on consultants than construction. Commission meetings reveal why.
brief: Escambia County has collected $47.2 million from stormwater fees since 2023 but completed just 12 of 89 planned drainage projects
County records show $8.4 million spent on engineering consultants, feasibility studies and project redesigns
Commission meetings reveal ongoing disputes over project prioritization between district commissioners
articles.body:
The intersection of Fairfield Drive and Michigan Avenue floods every time it rains more than two inches. Residents know to park on the high side of the street. They know which route to take when the water rises. They've known for years.

In November 2023, Escambia County voters approved a dedicated stormwater fee—$84 annually for the average homeowner—specifically to fix problems like this one. The Fairfield-Michigan drainage project ranked seventh on the county's priority list. Three years later, the intersection still floods. The project hasn't broken ground.

It isn't alone. County records obtained through a public records request show that of 89 drainage projects identified in the 2023 Stormwater Master Plan, just 12 have been completed. Another 14 are under construction. The remaining 63 exist only as line items on spreadsheets and engineering reports.

Meanwhile, the money keeps coming in. Since the fee took effect in January 2024, Escambia County has collected $47.2 million. Where it's gone explains why Fairfield Drive still floods.

The consulting carousel

County expenditure records show $8.4 million paid to engineering consultants since 2024. That's 18 percent of all stormwater revenue—more than the county has spent on actual construction.

The largest recipient is Jacobs Engineering, which holds the county's master stormwater contract. Jacobs has received $4.1 million for design work, project management and what county documents describe as "ongoing feasibility assessments."

Three projects have been redesigned at least twice. The Brownsville Road drainage improvement, originally estimated at $2.3 million, has accumulated $890,000 in engineering costs without a shovel touching dirt. County staff recommended the project be "re-scoped" in March 2025 after soil testing revealed conditions different from initial surveys.

"We're not going to rush into construction and have to tear it out," County Administrator Wes Moreno said at the April 2026 commission meeting. "These are complex systems. Getting it right the first time saves money in the long run."

The commission accepted this explanation without discussion.

District math

Watch enough Escambia County Commission meetings and a pattern emerges. When stormwater projects come up for approval, commissioners ask the same question: What's happening in my district?

The 2023 master plan ranked projects by a formula weighting flood frequency, property damage and population affected. District lines weren't part of the calculation. The top 20 projects clustered heavily in Districts 2 and 3—the county's most densely developed areas with the oldest drainage infrastructure.

This created a political problem. District 4 Commissioner Robert Bender raised it at the February 2025 budget workshop. "My constituents are paying this fee same as everyone else," Bender said, according to meeting minutes. "They deserve to see improvements in their neighborhoods too."

By May 2025, the commission had adopted an informal policy: each district would receive roughly equal stormwater spending regardless of the master plan rankings. Staff began reordering the project list.

The Fairfield-Michigan project dropped from seventh to nineteenth. A drainage improvement in Molino—a less flood-prone area in District 5—moved up to eighth.

Commissioner May Bell-Jolley, whose District 3 lost several high-priority projects in the reshuffling, objected at the time. "We did a master plan for a reason," she said. "We hired experts to tell us what needed fixing first."

She was outvoted 4-1.

The procurement bottleneck

Even projects that survive the political sorting face another obstacle: Escambia County's procurement process.

State law requires competitive bidding on projects over $300,000. County policy adds additional requirements—local vendor preferences, insurance minimums, bonding thresholds—that narrow the pool of eligible contractors.

For the Beulah Road culvert replacement, a $1.8 million project that did make it through, the county received just two bids. One was rejected for incomplete paperwork. The surviving bidder's price came in 34 percent over the engineer's estimate. Staff recommended accepting it anyway. The alternative was starting over.

"We don't have the contractor base we need," said David Forte, the county's public works director, at a June 2026 commission meeting. "Post-hurricane demand, labor shortages, same issues everyone's facing. Companies that can do this work are booked out 18 months."

Hurricane Helene's 2024 landfall near Tallahassee and the subsequent rebuilding effort pulled contractors east. Hurricane season 2025 brought near-misses that kept demand high. Escambia County competes for the same workers as Bay County, Walton County and the Florida Panhandle's tourism-driven construction boom.

What $47 million bought

The 12 completed projects aren't nothing. The Ninth Avenue outfall repair eliminated chronic flooding near Cordova Mall. Drainage improvements along Scenic Highway reduced runoff into Escambia Bay. A new retention pond in Brent serves a neighborhood that used to see standing water for days after storms.

But the math remains unfavorable. At the current completion rate—roughly four projects per year—the 2023 priority list won't be finished until 2042. And that assumes no new flooding problems emerge, no project costs increase and no additional political reshuffling.

The stormwater fee was sold to voters as a solution. Three years in, it looks more like a revenue stream in search of a delivery mechanism.

At the Fairfield-Michigan intersection, residents have stopped calling the county about flooding. "They know," said Marcus Webb, who has lived on Fairfield Drive for 11 years. "What else is there to say?"

The next commission discussion of stormwater priorities is scheduled for September. The Fairfield project isn't on the agenda.

articles.label: Feature
articles.headline: The Last Mobile Home Parks on Pensacola Beach
articles.dek: Hurricane Sally took out dozens of units. Rising land values and new flood maps are finishing the job. What happens to the people who've lived there for decades?
brief: Only two mobile home parks remain on Pensacola Beach, down from seven before Hurricane Ivan in 2004
New FEMA flood maps effective October 2026 will reclassify both parks as VE zones, requiring any rebuilt structures to meet coastal construction standards that mobile homes cannot satisfy
Longtime residents face displacement as land values exceed $2 million per acre and park owners weigh selling to developers
articles.body:
The wind chime hanging from Dot Hensley's awning is made of flattened spoons. She bent them herself in 1987, the year she moved her single-wide to Paradise Mobile Home Park on Via de Luna Drive. The chime has survived five hurricanes. Hensley is not sure she will survive the sixth.

"They keep telling me I need to have a plan," said Hensley, 79. She was sitting in a lawn chair under her carport on a Tuesday morning, watching a brown pelican dive into Santa Rosa Sound. "My plan was to die here. That was the whole plan."

Paradise is one of two mobile home parks still operating on Pensacola Beach. The other, Gulf Breeze Mobile Home Community, sits a quarter mile east on the same road. Together they hold 47 occupied units and roughly 80 full-time residents. Most are retirees. Some have lived there since the 1970s.

Both parks are out of time.

The math doesn't work anymore

Hurricane Sally made landfall on September 16, 2020, as a Category 2 storm. It moved slowly. The storm surge topped six feet in some sections of Pensacola Beach. At Paradise, 23 of 34 units sustained major damage. At Gulf Breeze Mobile Home Community, the number was 19 of 28.

Most were never replaced.

Current Escambia County land records show the Paradise property—3.1 acres with 180 feet of sound frontage—assessed at $6.2 million. The mobile homes sitting on that land are assessed collectively at $412,000. Gulf Breeze Mobile Home Community's 2.4 acres carry an assessment of $4.9 million.

"The land is worth more empty than full," said Marcus Webb, a commercial real estate broker with SVN Wertheim in Pensacola. "That's been true for a decade. The question was always when, not if."

The when appears to be now.

In March, FEMA released preliminary flood maps that will take effect October 1, 2026. Both parks currently sit in AE flood zones, which require structures to be elevated but allow manufactured housing with proper anchoring and foundation systems. The new maps reclassify the parcels as VE zones—velocity zones where wave action accompanies flooding.

VE zones require coastal construction standards. Load-bearing walls must be designed to withstand wave impact. Foundation systems must use pilings driven to specific depths. Mobile homes cannot meet these requirements.

Any unit destroyed more than 50% by a future storm cannot be rebuilt as a mobile home. Under Florida law, any unit removed from its lot for more than 180 days loses its grandfathered status.

"Once they're gone, they're gone," said Sarah Chen, a hazard mitigation specialist with the Florida Division of Emergency Management. "There's no mechanism in the current code to replace manufactured housing in a VE zone."

Thirty years of slow retreat

The beach once had seven mobile home parks.

Hurricane Ivan in 2004 destroyed two outright. One owner rebuilt as a boutique hotel. Another sold to a condo developer. Hurricane Dennis in 2005 took out a third. Two more closed between 2010 and 2015 as owners retired and chose to sell rather than reinvest.

What remains is a kind of afterimage. A handful of older residents in aging units, paying lot rents that have increased 40% since 2020, watching new construction rise around them.

The Pensacola Beach RV Resort, which opened in 2019, charges $125 per night for a standard site in summer. The starting price for a gulf-view condo at Portofino, two miles west, is $1.2 million.

Paradise charges $650 per month for lot rent. Gulf Breeze Mobile Home Community charges $575.

"It's the last affordable housing on the beach," said James Thornton, 68, who has lived at Gulf Breeze Mobile Home Community since 2003. "And I don't mean affordable housing like a program. I mean housing regular people can actually afford."

Thornton spent 30 years working as an electrician for Santa Rosa County. He is a veteran of the Navy, stationed at NAS Pensacola from 1976 to 1980. He bought his double-wide in 2003 for $42,000.

"Where am I supposed to go?" he said. "My whole life is here. My church is here. My doctor is here. My friends are here."

The owners

Paradise Mobile Home Park is owned by Via de Luna Properties LLC, a holding company registered to a Destin address. State corporate records list Thomas Kendrick Sr. as the registered agent. Kendrick, 84, did not respond to multiple requests for comment left at the registered address and through an attorney listed in previous litigation.

According to three current residents, Kendrick has not visited the property in at least two years. Day-to-day management is handled by his grandson, Thomas Kendrick III, who lives in Pensacola and visits weekly to collect rent and address maintenance issues.

The younger Kendrick agreed to speak briefly by phone but declined to be recorded.

"I can't tell you what the plan is because there isn't one yet," he said. "My grandfather is old. He's not in a position to make big decisions. For now, nothing's changing."

Asked specifically about the new flood maps and their implications, Kendrick said: "I'm aware of the situation."

Gulf Breeze Mobile Home Community is owned by Dorothy Pham, 71, who purchased the property in 1998 with her late husband. She lives in a double-wide on the premises and manages the park herself.

"Every year someone offers to buy me out," Pham said. She was standing in the small office she operates from a converted storage shed. A wall calendar showed a photograph of the park from 1999, when all 28 lots were full. "Last year a man from Texas offered $5 million. Cash. I said no."

Pham said she intends to keep operating as long as she can. But she acknowledged the flood maps present a problem she has not solved.

"If a big storm comes through, that's probably it," she said. "I can't rebuild these homes. The people here can't afford to rebuild them. And I'm not going to lie to anyone about that."

What options exist

Escambia County operates no relocation assistance program for displaced mobile home residents. The Florida Housing Finance Corporation offers down payment assistance for first-time homebuyers, but income limits exclude many retirees with Social Security benefits and pensions.

Section 8 housing vouchers, administered through the Escambia County Housing Finance Authority, carry a wait list of approximately 2,400 households. The authority has not opened its wait list to new applicants since 2019.

"There's a gap," said Rebecca Torres, director of the Pensacola Housing Authority. "These are people who aren't poor enough for subsidized housing and aren't wealthy enough for market-rate housing. They're in between. And there's not much in between anymore."

The Legal Services of North Florida office in Pensacola has begun tracking the situation. Staff attorney David Kim said his office has not yet received formal complaints from either park but expects to once the flood maps take effect.

"The scenario we're watching for is a storm that damages units beyond repair, and then residents find out they have no path to return," Kim said. "At that point, you're dealing with potential displacement of elderly, fixed-income residents with nowhere to go. That's a crisis."

A Thursday evening

On a Thursday in late July, a dozen residents of Paradise and Gulf Breeze Mobile Home Community gathered for a potluck dinner at the covered pavilion that sits between the two properties. The pavilion belongs to neither park—it was built by Santa Rosa Island Authority decades ago for public beach access that no longer exists, the path to the water long since blocked by private development.

Dot Hensley brought deviled eggs. James Thornton brought a cooler of beer. Dorothy Pham brought spring rolls she had made that morning.

The conversation turned, as it often does, to storms. To Ivan and Dennis and Sally. To the time in 2005 when the entire beach was closed for six weeks. To neighbors who left and never came back.

"We're the stubborn ones," said Hensley. "Or the stupid ones. Depends who you ask."

Later, as the sun dropped toward the sound, Hensley walked back to her single-wide. The spoon chime caught the breeze and rang out—a small, bright sound.

She paused at her door and looked back at the water.

"Forty years," she said. "Forty years of watching that same sunset. You can't take that from me. Even if you take everything else."

The Flightline will continue to follow this story as the October flood map deadline approaches. Residents of either park who wish to share their experiences can contact our newsroom at tips@theflightline.com.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's New Flight Pattern Brings Noise Complaints to East Hill
articles.dek: The Navy says training requirements changed. Residents say they weren't told. City officials say there's nothing they can do.
brief: Navy training aircraft began using a new flight pattern over East Hill in early July, routing T-6 Texan IIs directly over residential neighborhoods during morning and afternoon training blocks.
Residents report sustained noise levels they describe as significantly louder than previous years, with some homeowners logging 40 to 60 low-altitude passes per day.
City and county officials confirm they have no authority over military flight operations, leaving affected residents with few options beyond federal noise complaint channels.
articles.body:
The orange-and-white T-6 Texan II banked hard over 12th Avenue at 9:47 on a Tuesday morning, low enough that Margaret Hollis could read the numbers on its tail. She stood in her backyard on Strong Street, coffee going cold, counting. It was the fourteenth pass since 8 a.m.

"They've always flown around here," Hollis said. "This is different. This is over my house, every few minutes, all day long."

Since early July, residents across East Hill and North Hill have flooded the city with complaints about what they describe as a dramatic increase in aircraft noise from Naval Air Station Pensacola. The Navy confirms that training flight patterns changed this summer. What residents want to know is why they weren't told.

What Changed

NAS Pensacola serves as the primary training base for naval aviators, with student pilots logging thousands of flight hours annually in the single-engine T-6 Texan II. The aircraft has been a fixture in Pensacola skies for two decades.

Lt. Cmdr. Rachel Denton, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Training Command, said the pattern adjustment took effect July 7. She attributed the change to updated training requirements and airspace coordination with Pensacola International Airport.

"Training patterns are routinely evaluated and adjusted to meet mission requirements and ensure safety," Denton said in a written statement. "The current pattern supports the training timeline for student aviators while maintaining required separation from commercial traffic."

Denton declined to provide specifics about altitude minimums or the geographic boundaries of the new pattern, citing operational security. She said the Navy "remains committed to being a good neighbor" and encouraged residents to submit noise complaints through the base's community relations office.

The View from Below

David Chen has lived on Palafox Street in North Hill for 11 years. He works from home as a software developer. Since July 7, he has kept a log.

"Forty-seven passes on the 15th. Sixty-two on the 22nd," Chen said, scrolling through a spreadsheet on his laptop. "I'm not exaggerating. I started keeping track because I thought I was going crazy."

Chen estimated the aircraft pass at 500 to 800 feet above ground level, though he acknowledged he had no way to verify that. The Navy did not respond to a request for altitude data.

A noise meter app on Chen's phone registered peaks between 85 and 92 decibels during several passes. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration considers sustained exposure above 85 decibels potentially harmful to hearing.

"I'm not against the Navy. I'm not against the pilots," Chen said. "I just want to know why this changed and whether anyone considered the people who live here."

Similar complaints have surfaced on neighborhood social media groups and in calls to City Council offices. Council member Tenley Cobb, whose District 6 includes parts of East Hill, said she has received more than 200 emails and calls about aircraft noise since mid-July.

"People are frustrated, and I understand why," Cobb said. "But I have to be honest with them. The city has no jurisdiction over military flight operations. None."

A Jurisdictional Dead End

Federal law gives the military broad authority over airspace used for training. Local governments cannot regulate altitude, frequency or routing of military flights. Residents who want to file formal complaints must do so through the Department of Defense or the base's community relations office.

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh said his office has received similar complaints from residents near the Perdido Key and Warrington areas, though in lower numbers than the city.

"We're in the same boat as the city," Bergosh said. "We can pass along concerns. That's about it."

Bergosh said he planned to request a meeting with base leadership through the Defense Community Infrastructure Program, a federal initiative that facilitates communication between military installations and local governments. He did not provide a timeline.

The Navy's written statement noted that NAS Pensacola hosts periodic Community Plans and Liaison Officer meetings, though the next scheduled meeting is not until October.

What Residents Want

Back on Strong Street, Hollis said she isn't asking the Navy to stop flying. She wants two things: advance notice when patterns change and some limit on how many passes occur over residential areas in a single day.

"They sent us all those letters about the Blue Angels schedule," Hollis said, referring to mailings the Navy distributes before the annual air show. "They know how to communicate when they want to."

Hollis said she has lived in the same house since 1987. Her husband served 22 years in the Navy. She said she has always supported the base.

"But this feels like they forgot we're here," she said.

The T-6 came around again at 10:15. Hollis looked up, shielded her eyes from the sun and waited for the noise to pass. It took 11 seconds.

"Fifteen," she said.
